sections.overview: This fern-feeding noctuid moth occurs across parts of southern and central Europe and eastward through western Asia; records are local rather than uniformly common.
sections.identification: Adults have a wingspan of about 34–38 mm and patterned brown forewings; its names in several European languages refer to bracken, its characteristic larval food plant.
sections.habitat: It is recorded in deciduous and mixed woodland where bracken grows, including warm, fern-rich clearings and woodland margins.
sections.diet: The caterpillars feed on bracken (Pteridium aquilinum), rather than on the broad range of flowering plants used by many moth larvae.
sections.behavior: Adults fly mainly in early summer and may come to artificial light; in Britain it is only an occasional migrant, not a confirmed breeding resident.
sections.reproduction: In northern European accounts there is one summer generation, and the fully grown larva overwinters before pupating the following spring.
sections.ecology: Its specialised use of bracken links it to other fern-feeding Callopistria moths, but the consulted sources do not establish a particularly close sister species in the local bestiary.
sections.conservation: A Belgian regional assessment lists it as Near Threatened in Flanders; that local category should not be mistaken for a global IUCN assessment.
